transcripts.question: Give me Luke’s 30-second overview: who he is, what he’s shipped, and why it matters.
transcripts.raw:
Luke is a product designer who combines research, systems thinking, and technical prototyping to ship useful products, currently studying Computer Science with an HCI emphasis at BYU.

- **[Lucid](/work/lucid-ai)**: Designed an AI assistant that went from a blank page to general availability in 12 weeks, narrowing 20+ prototyped capabilities down to four core skills.
- **[Awardco](/work/awardco-login-flow-redesign)**: Redesigned login/authentication after telemetry showed password login succeeding only 34.6% of the time; usability testing showed a 78% reduction in decision time and a 4.5% increase in successful sign-ins. Handed off, not launched.
- **[Pattern](/work/pattern-custom-reports)**: Turned a small ticket into a nine-week Custom Reports redesign, validated in usability testing and shipped by the team after his internship.

My read: across all three, he grounds design decisions in evidence rather than assumptions.

[[followups]]
What was validated before the Awardco handoff?
What shipped at Lucid in 12 weeks?
How does Luke use code in the design process?

transcripts.question: Walk me through a difficult product decision Luke made: the tradeoff, what he chose, and how it played out.
transcripts.raw:
One clear example is from Awardco's login redesign.

**The tradeoff:** Testing showed password-first login was fastest (4.6 seconds to decide, slightly higher confidence) versus SSO-first (5.9 seconds). But password login was the method failing nearly two out of three times in the real product.

**What he chose:** Luke picked SSO-first anyway, reasoning that the fastest design wasn't the one most likely to help users actually sign in.

**How it played out:** In before-and-after usability testing, the redesigned system produced a 25% faster login, a 4.5% increase in successful sign-ins, and a 78% reduction in login-method decision time. The design passed security review and was handed off for implementation after his internship, so there's no production data on it yet.

[Awardco](/work/awardco-login-flow-redesign)

[[followups]]
Why did Luke choose the slower login design at Awardco?

transcripts.question: Did Luke reduce Awardco’s failed logins by 4.5%?
transcripts.raw:
Not quite. The 4.5% figure is a different metric in a different direction: in before-and-after usability testing, the redesigned login system produced a 4.5% increase in successful sign-ins, not a reduction in failed logins.

The baseline problem was separate: a year of company-wide login telemetry showed 7.7 million failed login attempts (6.7 million from password login alone) out of 45.9 million total attempts, with just 34.6% success for password login. That data motivated the redesign but isn't something the redesign is shown to have changed in production.

The usability testing also showed a 25% faster login and a 78% reduction in login-method decision time (27 seconds to 5.9 seconds). All of these are test results, not production metrics — the redesign was validated in testing and handed off for implementation after Luke's internship, with no post-launch data available.

More detail is in [Awardco](/work/awardco-login-flow-redesign).

[[followups]]
What was validated before the Awardco handoff?
Why did Luke choose the slower login design at Awardco?
What baseline problem motivated the Awardco redesign?

transcripts.question: What happened after Awardco launched?
transcripts.raw:
Awardco hadn't launched — the redesign was validated in usability testing and then handed off for implementation after Luke's internship ended. The portfolio doesn't have any post-launch, production, or live data for it.

What is verified:

**Testing results:** In before-and-after usability testing, the redesigned system showed a 25% faster login, a 4.5% increase in successful sign-ins, and a 78% reduction in login-method decision time (27 seconds down to 5.9 seconds), with higher confidence and lower reported difficulty. [Awardco](/work/awardco-login-flow-redesign)

**Handoff scope:** Completed designs for the SSO-first flow, the token-based approach that removes a second code entry, the mobile SMS verification flow, and the redesigned password-reset flow were all handed off for implementation, not launched by Luke.

**Why it matters:** The evidence Luke had was usability testing, not production telemetry, so the case study is careful to describe outcomes as validated rather than shipped.

The available portfolio evidence doesn't specify what happened after that handoff.

transcripts.question: Did Pattern test with 20 daily users?
transcripts.raw:
Not quite. Luke ran 20 usability sessions with 10 brand managers and 10 advertising strategists; the portfolio describes the participants by role, not by how often they used the product.

That testing showed brand managers editing charts while presenting to clients, which led Luke to remove the separate edit mode and combine viewing and editing into one experience — described as the most important change testing produced.

**Why it matters**

My read, based on the [Pattern](/work/pattern-custom-reports) case study, is that Luke used role-specific behavior observed in testing (not usage frequency) to justify a core interaction change, rather than guessing at what "power users" might want.

transcripts.question: Did Custom Reports save 400 hours per week?
transcripts.raw:
No — the portfolio doesn't verify any hours-saved figure for Custom Reports, at any number.

What it does show: building one client-ready report previously took 30–60 minutes across Predict, Excel, and slides, as a baseline problem before the redesign. There's no measured time-saved outcome tied to that baseline.

The redesign was validated in usability testing and shipped by the Pattern team after Luke's internship, but no post-launch time, adoption, or productivity metric is documented in the case study.

**Why it matters**

My read, based on the [Pattern](/work/pattern-custom-reports) case study, is that Luke's next step was proposed rather than measured: he wanted to check whether users returned to build a second report, since only about 15% of eligible users had returned in the feature's first year before the redesign.

transcripts.question: What was Lucid AI’s adoption rate?
transcripts.raw:
The available portfolio evidence doesn't specify that. Luke's internship ended shortly after the assistant's general-availability release, so the case study doesn't include long-term adoption, usage, or retention data.

What the evidence does show is the shipping timeline and scope: the assistant went from a blank page to general availability in 12 weeks, reaching internal users on July 20 and all Lucid tiers on August 5. The four shipped skills were Find docs, Summarize, Build a diagram, and Catch up, narrowed down from more than 20 prototyped capabilities tested with 12 external user sessions.

Before Luke left, he also designed and handed off an A/B test comparing the side-panel and full-page experiences, but no results from that test are available either.

For more on what shipped and what was tested, see [Lucid](/work/lucid-ai).
